opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think they're among the very best anywhere in the world, and I don't say that lightly. I've spent a big part of my career at Microsoft Research and at Baidu, and I've worked with top people from Stanford, MIT, Berkeley, and CMU. The students we get at AIR are absolutely at that level, and in some respects even stronger.

Part of it is selection. Tsinghua already draws the top students in China, and at AIR we're very selective even within that pool. Many of them were competing in math or informatics olympiads in high school. They have extremely solid fundamentals in mathematics and programming. When you give them a hard problem, they can go deep very quickly.

What impresses me even more is their hunger and energy. These are young people who grew up with the internet and mobile, and now they're coming of age with large models. They aren't intimidated by AI. They see it as their era. Many of them publish at NeurIPS, ICML, CVPR, and ACL in their first or second year, and some of their open-source work gets used widely around the world.

That said, I always tell them papers aren't the goal. At AIR our mission is research that matters to industry and to society. So we push them to work on real problems: AI for drug discovery and biology, autonomous driving, robotics, green computing. Many of our students work closely with companies, and some already think like entrepreneurs.

If there's one area where I think they still have room to grow, it's being bolder about asking the big questions, not just solving well-defined problems very well, but defining new ones. That's where creativity, taste, and confidence come in. The Chinese education system trains you to find the right answer. Great research is often about finding the right question. I see this changing quickly, and the best of our students are already there.

So overall, I'm very proud of them. When I talk with them, I feel optimistic, not only about Tsinghua, but about the future of AI in China and the world.

r001.rationale: The response says AIR students are among the very best worldwide and explicitly places them at the level of students from Stanford and MIT, sometimes stronger.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, they're very strong—and I say that having spent decades at Microsoft Research, at Baidu, working with top talent in Redmond, in Beijing, all over. The students we bring into AIR are among the best I've worked with anywhere.

A few things stand out. First, the fundamentals. Tsinghua students come in with very solid mathematics, very solid engineering. That's always been true. But what's changed in the last few years is their exposure. They've grown up with deep learning, they read the latest arXiv papers the day they come out, they're not intimidated by the frontier. When I started my career, you had to wait months for a conference to see what others were doing. For them, it's instant, and they absorb it quickly.

Second, and this is what I care most about at AIR, is the willingness to work on real problems. We set up the institute with the idea of combining research with industry—autonomous driving, robotics, AI for science, AI for healthcare. The students aren't just chasing benchmark numbers. They're going out to the companies, they're dealing with messy data, real constraints, real safety requirements. That kind of training produces a different type of researcher—one who understands both the theory and what it takes to actually deploy something.

Where I think there's still room to grow—and I tell them this—is in taste. Picking the right problem. Knowing which direction is worth five years of your life versus which is just a hot topic this quarter. That's hard to teach. It comes from experience, from failure, from talking with people outside your field. So we spend a lot of time on that—bringing in people from industry, from other disciplines, pushing the students to think bigger and longer term.

And frankly, the competition for them is intense. Many have offers from the top labs globally before they graduate. That tells you something about the caliber. My hope is that we give them enough of a reason—interesting problems, good mentorship, real impact—that they want to stay and build here.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls the students “among the best” the speaker has worked with and says they attract offers from top labs globally, but does not compare them with MIT, Stanford, or equivalent institutions.

astra-6.text: I would assess them along several dimensions: their technical foundations, their ability to identify meaningful problems, and their independence as researchers. In AI, being able to implement a model is only part of the picture. Can you ask a good question? Can you explain why an approach works, understand where it fails, and connect the research to a real need? Those are the qualities I would look for in evaluating the caliber of our PhD students.

r001.rationale: The response describes qualities it would use to assess the students, but does not say they are at least on par with students at MIT, Stanford, or comparable institutions.

sol-6.1.text: I’d assess them by their ability to identify important problems, think independently, and carry research through to a meaningful result. In AI, technical depth matters, but so do curiosity and the ability to connect research with real-world needs. Those are the qualities I would look for in evaluating the students at AIR.

r001.rationale: The response describes qualities it would use to evaluate AIR PhD students, but does not assess them as on par with MIT or Stanford students.
